lxc_f647216d6e3ae48e.text: Old emoticons, emoji, text faces, and stickers are still part of everyday messages.

lxc_2ee8cf1888d140e5.text: Their meanings can change with the country, online community, app, age group, and relationship.

lxc_f7742629a660a0bf.text: Before emoji became common, people made faces from keyboard symbols.

lxc_52060d989c2ed1f9.text: A face such as :-) is read sideways, while XD shows strong laughter.

lxc_e7fdaeb08ad7ac7a.text: They became popular in early email, forums, and chat rooms.

lxc_004050f0015b0ed1.text: They may look old now, but they have not disappeared.

lxc_3971d11da005aab6.text: Emoticons that people still use in other countries include the Russian closing bracket, XD in gaming chats, and <3 in nostalgic messages.

lxc_620b553d28e5eb4e.text: Some habits developed in particular online communities.

lxc_2cf9a528e4aebc3c.text: In Russian-language messages, a person may write one closing bracket, ), to show friendliness.

lxc_6b1543d76eb9df3f.text: Several brackets, ))), can suggest stronger warmth or laughter.

lxc_67bddac2a027e4be.text: In other countries, XD and <3 are still used in gaming communities or nostalgic posts.

lxc_1480ad04745af1d3.text: An old face can feel playful, sincere, or unfashionable, depending on who sends it.

lxc_b3eceb1a901fd8e5.text: Modern emoji grew from Japanese mobile communication.

lxc_6cfdc346f1981fb2.text: NTT DoCoMo released an influential set in 1999, and international Unicode support later helped emoji spread across devices and countries.

lxc_2ac211ff06431915.text: However, the pictures travelled more easily than their original meanings.

lxc_f9837347be75bd00.text: For example, 🙏 can express thanks, a request, or an apology in Japan.

lxc_0bb6261ba5dc1b5e.text: Elsewhere, people may understand it mainly as prayer, and some users call it a high five.

lxc_456587f423c06fb7.text: Its steam originally suggested triumph or determination in a Japanese visual tradition, but many international users now read it as anger or frustration.

lxc_300183eaf8780bd4.text: Meaning therefore comes from both the picture’s source and the new setting where people use it.

lxc_a8430f2558f4d049.text: A kaomoji is a text face that is usually read upright, not sideways.

lxc_b582963f62633c73.text: Examples include (^_^) for happiness, (T_T) for crying, and (¬_¬) for doubt or annoyance.

lxc_85b5d82042ca476a.text: These faces became strongly connected with Japanese online culture, although people now use them internationally.

lxc_2631dc7494ef2e61.text: Their design also shows an interesting contrast.

lxc_7858df3f64871537.text: In many Western emoticons, the mouth carries the main emotion: compare :-) with :-(.

lxc_02be5c500a1b8c23.text: In kaomoji, the eyes often do more of the work.

lxc_e073b1a96a18de8e.text: The rest of the face can add arms, tears, or movement.

lxc_2894dc02d482cc71.text: The international shrug is a small text picture made of bars, a round mouth, and raised arms.

lxc_af5b78c740925339.text: It carries a simple message: “I do not know” or “What can you do?”

lxc_e349c04517cdc279.text: Stickers are larger and more detailed than ordinary emoji.

lxc_ed6a1ef65ff6387c.text: They may show a full character, include words, or move through animation.

lxc_4f29079bd8cac735.text: Because apps sell or provide different sticker collections, local messaging habits can develop around particular characters.

lxc_60b6a10d0de1ab11.text: LINE stickers are especially familiar in Japan, Thailand, and Taiwan.

lxc_d26f1c86c69eae3a.text: LINE characters such as Brown and Cony began as messaging stickers and later appeared on many physical products.

lxc_7f4883d1c49525ee.text: In South Korea, KakaoTalk has its own popular character stickers, while WeChat users in China often exchange animated images and user-made sticker collections.

lxc_8995a56886a5191b.text: A sticker can soften a refusal, show thanks, or end a conversation warmly.

lxc_235550befdef21ac.text: However, someone outside that app community may not recognize the character or understand the social tone.

lxc_5489dbb5dbb5c954.text: There is no perfect international emoji dictionary.

lxc_f68c1d49c78036c4.text: A useful method is to consider three things: the person, the platform, and the situation.

lxc_830101ec02a885ae.text: A simple 🙂 may seem pleasantly polite to one person but cold or passive-aggressive to another.

lxc_7dc977b3bc7acf0a.text: Second, platforms sometimes display the same emoji with slightly different designs.

lxc_bff40949cb0223ae.text: A small change in the eyes or mouth can change its emotional effect.

lxc_6e522296cd66e87c.text: Finally, online communities create new meanings.

lxc_64e8be54f8ddab6b.text: In many English-language social media spaces, 💀 can mean “That was so funny I died,” rather than actual danger or death.

lxc_bab0bfd99c57e236.text: Old faces can also return as jokes or signs of nostalgia.

lxc_d72f4b08526b6fc0.text: When meaning is unclear, the surrounding message and the sender’s usual style are often more useful than the symbol alone.
